structuredContent.content:
﻿LANE 1 — HOUSEHOLD + QUICK COMMERCE
Start 14 Oct 2026 | India metro-first | Ownership: This document only
Mission: falsify or substantiate FOOD-01 and FOOD-02 at the actual household-decision level. Study purchases, kitchen inventory, delivery, family members' plans, food consumed and actually weighed edible waste. B2C/partner route is secondary to harm. Read Research Control Room before each run.


HYPOTHESIS FOOD-01 — MULTI-PERSON FOOD COORDINATION
People: independent grocery shopper(s), cook, parents, roommates, elders, children, food-delivery consumer; decisions shift after work, school, visitor or meal cancellation. Current evidence: Delhi 56-household audit documents planning, overcooking and changed routines as drivers. Claim of unresolved software gap: UNPROVEN. Compete with NoWaste, Samsung Food, WhatsApp/shared list/calendar and ordinary Gemini. Tests: actual episodes, user effort/time, measurable edible kg; do not assume system can know fridge contents without evidence.


HYPOTHESIS FOOD-02 — QUICK-COMMERCE RELATION TO WASTE
Platforms to inspect: Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, BigBasket/bbnow; plus Swiggy/Zomato restaurant ordering, kiranas and supermarkets. Redseer FY2024 ~6 orders/month among monthly transacting quick-commerce users; metro skew; data does not demonstrate waste consequences. Counter-hypothesis: rapid small orders could reduce overbuying, while promotion-driven extras may increase waste. Need purchase & discard measures with denominator and confounder awareness. Shopping integration/auto checkout is speculative without authentic authorized APIs + consent.


RESEARCH QUEUE
1. Deep incumbent feature audit with dated official documentation and independent complaints if corroborated.
2. Scope authentic anonymized multi-channel household purchase artifacts and feasible consent process.
3. Identify real-life disruption cases with observed duplicate buys, overcooking and wasted perishables; find credible empirical studies (India, Japan, Singapore, Australia, other JAPAC).
4. Evaluate AI orchestration, memory/state (consented), tool calling, voice/image/receipts, grounded healthy/sustainable choices, price comparisons; contrast deterministic rules and ordinary LLM.
5. Falsification: if baseline shared-list/NoWaste/Samsung Food performs equivalently in real cases, downgrade. Measure edible kg, cost, effort and retention, not engagement only.


CURRENT VERDICT: FOOD-01 ADVANCE TO COMPARATIVE TEST; FOOD-02 NARROW CAUSAL EVIDENCE UNKNOWN. Benchmark NOT RUN.
SOURCE STARTERS
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0950329325003064
https://redseer.com/articles/indias-q-commerce-ascent-a-new-era-in-shopping/
https://www.nowasteapp.com/home/
https://support.samsungfood.com/hc/en-us/articles/35369657798548-Getting-Started-with-Meal-Planner
https://www.swiggy.com/corporate/press-release/how-india-swiggyd-2025-a-feast-for-the-fast-the-foodie-and-the-future/
APPEND DATED RUN ENTRIES BELOW. Keep earlier findings and counterfindings; no fabricated tests.




14 OCT 2026 — LANE 1, RUN 01: NEW EVIDENCE AND RESEARCH DECISIONS
FOOD-02: QUICK COMMERCE MUST BE SEGMENTED BY PURCHASE MISSION. A Grant Thornton Bharat 2026 survey, reported by PTI on 7 April, covered over 1,600 consumers and 1,000 kirana retailers in Indian metros and smaller cities. Reported usage motives: 45% urgent purchases, 24% daily top-ups, 19% impulse purchases. These are survey responses, not measured waste, and original questionnaire/weighting was not available. Source: https://money.rediff.com/amp/news/market/convenience-drives-retail-choices-in-india-report/44897720260407 . Hypothesis: urgent top-ups may reduce bulk spoilage; impulse buying may have different effects. No causal evidence yet. Verdict: NARROW. Kill if real discarded edible food does not differ after controlling for household characteristics.


FOOD-02 FRESH PRODUCE CHANNELS: LocalCircles original survey published 24 Nov 2023, fielded Sep–Nov 2023, >24,000 question responses across 297 Indian districts. Of 12,207 respondents asked where they bought MOST household fruits and vegetables, only 7% chose online grocery, while 45% chose local markets, 21% weekly markets and 19% neighbourhood vendors. Among 11,964 responses to a separate multiple-choice online-produce problems question, 73% selected low quality, 56% high prices, 51% difficult returns, 37% inconsistent availability. Source: https://www.localcircles.com/a/press/page/grocery-platforms-survey . Caveat: self-selected platform respondents; 2023, not a 2026 population estimate. The 7% is PRIMARY channel, not whether respondents ever buy online. Complaints are not measured spoilage. This challenges an app centered only on online order receipts. Potential unmet failure: short-lived produce arriving in poor condition, but supplier quality/returns rather than GenAI may dominate. Verdict: NARROW. Proposed falsification (NOT RUN): 30 paired produce purchase lines from delivery and local markets, recording arrival condition, shelf life, consumed/discarded edible grams, price, and existing refund outcome. Kill if actual discard is unaffected or ordinary quality control is adequate.


FOOD-02 ADJACENT ENVIRONMENTAL LEVER: Eshtiyagh et al. (preprint 21 Oct 2025) analyzed 6,362,860 express grocery orders from Dubai (2023) and 2,169,520 scheduled orders (2022), total 8,532,380. A dispatch/bundling simulation using these records estimated that about five additional minutes could reduce daily delivery mileage by ~30% and modeled lifecycle carbon emissions by ~20% in tested conditions. This was not an observed intervention, an India estimate, a reduction in discarded food, or a demonstrated AI benefit. Peer review unconfirmed. Original: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19066 . Verdict: NARROW as a logistics-emissions hypothesis separate from food waste. Main objection: established operations-research routing may be sufficient; household apps lack dispatch authority.


Research status: FOOD-02 remains NARROW; food waste effect unmeasured.


Further counterevidence: Existing grocery services already provide scheduled delivery choices in some locations. Delivery-window selection is not itself a novel product feature. The original source was a September 2026 industry report; availability in the selected metro needs verification. Conventional routing remains the baseline comparator.


Next research gate (NOT RUN): collect consented grocery purchase receipts, purchase mission, changes in household meal plans and weighed edible discard for a small urban household sample. Compare results against ordinary shared lists, NoWaste, Samsung Food and a general LLM. Analyze actual food discarded rather than order counts. Track grocery spending, time burden and any delivery-emissions scenario separately. FOOD-01 remains ADVANCE TO COMPARATIVE TEST; FOOD-02 remains NARROW. Strongest kill criterion: no meaningful residual failure beyond existing tools, or purchase channel does not predict avoidable waste after accounting for household differences. Project Problem Value /100 and judging scores withheld until this is tested.




14 OCT 2026 — LANE 1, RUN 02: ONLINE VEGETABLE SHOPPING AND THE FIRST-WASTE EVENT (NEW ORIGINAL EVIDENCE)


PRIMARY NEW FINDING — FOOD-02: A PEER-REVIEWED CHANNEL COMPARISON FINDS AN ASSOCIATION WITH MORE VEGETABLE WASTE, BUT NOT A QUICK-COMMERCE CAUSAL EFFECT.
Tian, Lin, Gao, Yu and Li, “From markets to clicks: The impact of purchasing channel migration on household food waste,” Waste Management 204:114908; published online 29 May 2025, issue 1 Aug 2025, DOI 10.1016/j.wasman.2025.114908. Original source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40446430/ . Geography: China, household vegetable consumption. Abstract reports online purchases associated with +12.967 grams vegetable waste, +0.017 waste proportion, and +0.121 higher probability of ANY waste compared with offline purchasing. The association was statistically apparent for leafy and root vegetables, not fruit vegetables. Increased risk of waste attributed to expiration (+0.125) and improper storage (+0.072) in the model. Crucially, among households that ALREADY wasted vegetables, there was no significant difference in waste amount/proportion between purchasing channels. This suggests the actionable hypothesis might be preventing the first avoidable spoilage incident, rather than reducing waste volume among all existing wasters.


EVIDENCE LIMITS: Full article methodology and sampling denominator not accessible in this research pass: UNKNOWN; units/time base of +12.967 g not sufficiently specified in the abstract; DO NOT present it as grams per household-week/order or extrapolate it to India. The abstract uses causal language, but identification strategy and selection/confounding controls cannot be independently audited here. Online grocery in China is NOT identical to 10-minute quick commerce in India. 0.121 is a model-reported probability change, not a measured India quick-commerce effect. No physical weighing method was verified from abstract; classify measurement mode UNKNOWN. Evidence confidence MEDIUM for reported study findings, LOW for India causal transfer.


NEW RESEARCH QUESTION / SPECIFIC USER TASK: A metro grocery buyer receives online leafy/root vegetables; other household members decide meals, and produce remains unused because shelf-life and storage decisions were not aligned with changing meal attendance. Can a household reliably identify and act on a vulnerable batch BEFORE the first spoilage event, beyond a receipt reminder, simple storage label, shared list, NoWaste or Samsung Food? Current evidence supports possible failure at storage/expiration, NOT that cross-app ordering is its cause. A photo alone cannot certify freshness or remaining safe shelf life.


INDEPENDENT BEHAVIORAL CORROBORATION, DISTINCT CHANNEL: Shamim and Misra, “Unravelling the dynamics of food waste and food delivery apps: insights from SEM and FSQCA,” British Food Journal 127(11):4077–4091 (2025), DOI 10.1108/BFJ-11-2024-1226, publisher issue: https://www.emerald.com/bfj/issue/127/11 ; indexed abstract: https://ouci.dntb.gov.ua/en/works/7WjmqN1L/ . Sample: 344 online food-delivery app users, online survey; geography NOT verified in accessible abstract. Structural equation modeling finds hedonic value associated with over-ordering, which is associated with reported food waste; personalization associated with hedonic value but not functional value. This concerns PREPARED MEAL DELIVERY, not online groceries or household inventory; self-report/SEM associations are NOT verified grams or proof that platform design causes waste. It independently suggests an additional purchase-stage behavioral mechanism but must not be combined with the vegetable-waste coefficient. Evidence confidence MEDIUM for described correlations, LOW for causal interpretation or transfer to Indian metros.


COMPETITION AND COUNTEREVIDENCE: NoWaste and Samsung Food already advertise expiry reminders, inventory, shopping lists, meal planning and recipe recommendations; WhatsApp and shared calendars handle changing attendance, and ordinary Gemini can explain storage guidelines and suggest ingredient use. Traditional refrigerator organization in the 2025 Japan 119-household intervention performed at least comparably to an app in short-run waste reduction; do not assume AI outperforms physical visibility. Online top-up purchasing might reduce bulk spoilage, and Chinese channel associations could reflect buyer selection, product quality or packaging. Existing apps may already address the proposed incident; no head-to-head run.


AI ROLE (CONDITIONAL, NOT A SOLUTION COMMITMENT): Gemini could reconcile user-consented purchase artifacts, household schedule changes and structured product facts, maintain auditable per-item state, invoke permitted reminder/checkout tools with explicit authorization, and ground food-storage advice in authoritative sources. Actual spoilage-risk thresholds, purchased quantities, dates and budget should use verified data plus deterministic rules. A standard reminder or visible refrigerator organizer is the baseline; agents/memory only matter if they demonstrably reduce missed interventions and user effort. No official general consumer checkout integration with Blinkit/Zepto/Instamart verified; automation remains blocked on access/authorization. No new Gemini feature tested.


FALSIFIABLE STUDY DESIGN — NOT RUN: 15–30 consenting Indian metro households over 3–4 weeks, ideally pre-registered, capturing online/offline vegetable batches separately (leafy, root, fruit vegetables), purchase weight/price/channel/date, freshness at arrival, packaging/storage, planned vs actual meals, edible grams discarded with reason/date and actual consumption. Compare (A) ordinary shared list + visible storage guidance, (B) NoWaste/Samsung Food or equivalent, (C) ordinary Gemini conversation, and (D) any new workflow ONLY after it is built; use within-household comparisons or randomization if feasible, not mere cross-sectional channel correlation. Primary outcome: probability of any avoidable edible spoilage event per purchased produce batch and grams wasted / grams purchased; secondary: grams/household-week, INR discarded, household time/steps, accuracy of item state, and any net environmental savings estimated conservatively by produce category and disposal path. Control for household size, storage, purchased quantity, product quality and cooking frequency. This is a PROPOSED test, not evidence that data or participants exist.


DECISION: FOOD-02 stays NARROW but now has a specific independent published signal for online vegetable expiration/storage; FOOD-01 stays ADVANCE TO COMPARATIVE TEST because multi-person coordination remains plausible but unproven after incumbent tools. Do NOT advance to an automated purchasing product or score /100: frequency of residual unmet incident, workaround cost, data access, actual effect and GenAI advantage remain UNKNOWN. Hackathon 40/25/25/10 readiness also NOT SCORED. Strongest rejection: basic storage guidance, fridge organization or existing apps perform equally well, or product quality/household behavior dominates information, so an AI workflow cannot credibly prevent discarded edible grams. Revisit only with genuine Indian paired purchase-to-disposal evidence or a valid incumbent comparison.


14 OCT 2026 — LANE 1 RUN 03: NEW EVIDENCE — INDIA ONLINE GROCERY OVER-ORDERING
Jasrotia et al., SN Business & Economics 6(10), October 2026, DOI 10.1007/s43546-026-01458-1; https://ideas.repec.org/a/spr/snbeco/v6y2026i10d10.1007_s43546-026-01458-1.html . Original Indian survey of 363 online grocery shoppers analyzed by PLS-SEM found perceived value associated with impulse buying and over-ordering; wider assortment and price value related to perceived value. Convenience moderation was not supported. This is an India-specific purchase mechanism, NOT measured edible food waste, not quick-commerce-specific, not a representative household sample, and not causal experimental evidence. Full methods inaccessible here. Confidence MEDIUM for survey associations, LOW for discarded-food inference. FOOD-02 NARROW: test whether promotion-driven over-orders of perishable food are actually discarded, after comparing urgent/top-up orders, kirana and supermarket purchases. Strongest rejection: purchases are consumed or stockpiled and do not create additional avoidable food waste.


14 OCT 2026 — LANE 1 RUN 03: NEW NON-GENAI CONTROL AND EVIDENCE GATE
Seta et al., “Effects of a gamified self-monitoring app on household food waste reduction,” Detritus 35:23–41, available online 26 May 2026; original journal https://digital.detritusjournal.com/articles/effects-of-a-gamified-self-monitoring-app-on-household-food-waste-reduction/5732 ; DOI 10.31025/2611-4135/2026.19596 . Japan intervention involving 126 households assigned to intervention/control, with cloud-connected weighing of separately discarded avoidable food across three two-week measurement periods (baseline, intervention, three-month follow-up). A non-GenAI gamified behavior app prompted searching for food needing use, moving it visibly, using it and finishing meals. Reported average weekly household avoidable waste fell by 190 g (45%) in intervention vs 60 g (13%) control, a 32-percentage-point difference in within-group percentage declines, not a demonstrated AI saving. Baseline-adjusted bootstrap GLM found a statistically significant intervention/control difference. Abstract does NOT resolve long-term follow-up persistence or which behavior mediated the result; behavior-change indicators were not significantly associated with waste changes in the main-effects model. Over 90% of intervention participants used the app five or more days per week, but long-run adoption is unknown. Confidence HIGH for sample's physically measured contrast, LOW for generalizing to Indian metros or proving GenAI value. This is a stronger competitor than a generic inventory app and raises the evidence bar for FOOD-01.
Independent adjacent mechanism, NOT pooled with groceries: Rahman et al., Food and Humanity 5:100886 (Dec 2025), DOI 10.1016/j.foohum.2025.100886, original university publication https://scholar.ub.ac.id/en/publications/do-online-food-delivery-platforms-contribute-to-food-waste-eviden/ . Cross-sectional model using 1,042 Indonesian university respondents associated prepared-meal delivery frequency with reported waste and over-ordering; this is not Indian quick commerce, not verified physical weights, and not randomized causal evidence.
Next falsification (NOT RUN): For consenting metro households compare real purchase motives (urgent/top-up vs promotion/impulse) and low-tech use-first refrigerator zones/basic reminders vs NoWaste/Samsung Food/shared lists and ordinary Gemini, recording receipt quantity, purchase price, meal changes, actual edible grams discarded per purchased edible gram, first spoilage events per batch, time spent and fridge conditions. Only test a proposed Gemini agent after baseline alternatives; use grounded structured data, consented household state and explicit authorization for any external checkout. Rules may outperform an agent for expiry reminders and duplicate purchases. No partner checkout API, study participants or product effects verified. FOOD-01 ADVANCE TO COMPARATIVE VALIDATION; FOOD-02 NARROW, causality unresolved. Problem Value /100 and official 40/25/25/10 hackathon scores WITHHELD. Strongest FOOD-01 rejection: simple visibility and habit changes match any AI approach at lower effort; strongest FOOD-02 rejection: no incremental edible discard after adjusting for household traits and item quality.




14 OCT 2026 — LANE 1 RUN 04: CAUSAL PROMOTION EXPERIMENT + SHOPPING-FREQUENCY COUNTERMODEL (NEW EVIDENCE)
FOOD-02 NEW STRONGER ORIGINAL EVIDENCE: MULTI-UNIT PROMOTIONS CAN CAUSE EXTRA PERISHABLE PURCHASES, BUT DIRECT PHYSICAL FOOD-WASTE IMPACT REMAINS UNMEASURED.
Gravert, Christina and Mormann, Milica, “In-store food promotions increase sales as well as household food waste,” Scientific Reports 15, 18035, published 23 May 2025. ORIGINAL OPEN ARTICLE: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-01800-x . Underlying public data and analysis code: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/7NSBP (authors report availability; files NOT downloaded or audited here). Actual natural field experiment: eight supermarkets from two chains in SWEDEN, 8–21 March 2021, with 43,246 units of cucumber/broccoli sold. The article was published in 2025; data were collected in 2021. Retail displays were randomized across store/time in an A-B-A design, with the same effective unit price. Multi-unit “2 for X” framing increased units sold by 19.5% relative to “1 for X/2” (p<0.001). A simple consumption-oriented prompt reduced units purchased 10.8% vs multi-unit framing, and a salient single-item comparison price reduced units 9.1% (both p<0.001). These are SALES quantity changes, NOT measured avoided food waste. Critically, simple non-AI nudges worked, setting a high bar for any GenAI cart advisor.
Follow-up: QR stickers were attached to 21,000 vegetables; 178 shoppers completed a one-week consumption follow-up (~1% response); 176 retained after excluding two who said they bought zero. Of the 121 respondents buying at least two items, 12% in the multi-unit condition vs 0% in the single-unit-discount condition reported not fully consuming purchased food (p=0.064, so NOT significant at conventional 5% threshold); 15% prompt and 6% salience groups also reported not fully consuming. This was self-reported BINARY full consumption, not weighed edible waste, and does NOT definitively establish food disposal; low follow-up response and small treatment cells limit waste inference. A separate preregistered US online hypothetical shopping experiment recruited 397, analyzed 389 after attention check; respondents given two-for-one broccoli scenario rated perceived waste likelihood 54.73/100 vs 42.07/100 for a single broccoli at 50% discount (p=0.021), and 34.19/100 for one regular-priced (p<0.001). This is INTENTION/PERCEIVED RISK, not physical waste. Strong causal evidence for PURCHASE framing effect, weaker for actual disposal, and no direct Indian q-commerce evidence.
RESEARCH INTERPRETATION (NOT A RESULT): The key decision may be “Should I add a second short-shelf-life unit because of an offer?” rather than “What should I cook?” This occurs before purchasing and can be shared across kiranas, supermarkets, Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart, but evidence does not show any named Indian platform deploys the same perishable multi-unit mechanism at scale. Compare offers actually observed in one metro, never infer from platform category or discount campaigns. The retailer has a potential incentive conflict: more units sold vs fewer discarded by households. The cheapest competitor is an accurate per-unit price and one-line “will this be used?” nudge, not a GenAI agent. A platform partner's willingness to change cart design is UNKNOWN.
FOOD-01 + FOOD-02 IMPORTANT CONTRARIAN 2025 MODEL: van Rooijen, Gerdessen, Claassen and de Leeuw, “Meal planning under uncertainty: How shopping frequency affects food waste,” Sustainable Production and Consumption 57:403–412, published July 2025; original university record https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/meal-planning-under-uncertainty-how-shopping-frequency-affects-fo/ ; DOI https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spc.2025.05.015 ; full open repository PDF https://edepot.wur.nl/694932 . The researchers built a ROLLING-HORIZON MATHEMATICAL OPTIMIZATION model of a four-person household over 21 days with low, medium and high uncertainty in dinner attendance, considering package sizes, nutrition and recipe selection. Across shopping frequencies, MODELLED food waste ranged 0–52 g, 46–300 g and 50–900 g per 21 days for low/medium/high uncertainty, respectively; these are scenario outputs, NOT measured household waste or real-world effect sizes. In the model, more frequent shopping can reduce waste when meal attendance is uncertain, while less frequent coordinated shopping may suit stable households. Selecting recipes based on existing stock reduced simulated waste to about 3 g/day across uncertainty levels. Thus “frequent q-commerce is wasteful” is an invalid blanket assumption. A conditional choice of shopping frequency and quantities is a more defensible research question. The paper demonstrates NON-GENAI operations research already covers a large part of the decision logic, so any Gemini advantage must be in collecting changing attendance/intent with less friction and connecting reliable context, not mathematical meal optimization alone.
NEW CROSS-SOURCE INSIGHT: The 2025 Swedish randomized purchase-framing experiment supports a causal retail decision lever, while the 2025 Netherlands mathematical model supports a countervailing benefit from flexible small purchases under uncertain meal attendance. These are different countries, settings, methods and outcome types; they cannot be pooled into a single expected India reduction or carbon figure. Combined, they argue for a nuanced taxonomy: (A) demand-matched urgent top-up; (B) deliberate multi-day stock-up; (C) promotion-induced extra perishables; (D) planned short-life markdown purchase. Only category C has the new controlled promotion evidence, and even there physically weighed waste remains UNKNOWN.
COMPETITION: NoWaste and Samsung Food already provide pantry lists, meal planning and inventory features; WhatsApp/Calendar communicate attendance, ordinary Gemini can reason about quantity and offer arithmetic. The Swedish trial shows a plain unit-price display and text nudge can alter purchasing; Wageningen shows deterministic rolling-horizon optimization can model uncertain meal demand. A differentiator requiring GenAI/agents/memory is NOT established. An authorized purchase or cart-modification API for Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart, BigBasket or Swiggy/Zomato has NOT been verified; no automatic buying should be claimed.
MEASUREMENT AND ACCESS: The Gravert/Mormann authors explicitly publish underlying experiment data/code on OSF (access/rights to be checked before use); this enables reproducibility of purchase effects, NOT Indian grocery waste. No Indian household consented receipts, offer screenshots, purchase/consumption logs or weighed edible disposal records available yet. To evaluate environmental/social severity measure edible grams discarded / edible grams purchased by category, INR paid for discarded food, meal attendance uncertainty, effort, package size, and actual delivery/packaging footprint. For any CO2e/water use food- and region-specific factors and counterfactual substitution; do not count reduced purchases as automatically reduced emissions without inventory response.
FALSIFIABLE NEXT TEST (NOT RUN): (1) Audit 100 current real perishable offer cards from one selected Indian metro across quick commerce AND kiranas/supermarkets, recording actual single vs multi-unit effective unit price, quantity constraints, expiration/freshness, promo type and whether cart controls can be changed; platform terms respected, no scraping. (2) Recruit consenting households with varying meal-attendance uncertainty; track purchase intent, order receipts, actual edible grams consumed/discarded per item/batch over 3–4 weeks. (3) Compare randomized basic unit-price + one-line nudge against existing inventory app/shared list and ordinary Gemini; only then test a consented context-aware agent. (4) Pre-register two distinct hypotheses: promotions increase quantity (purchase effect) and promotions increase physically discarded edible mass (waste effect), accounting for actual package size, price, freshness and meal attendance. Reject if India offers lack multi-unit framing, if added food is consumed, if simple nudge is equivalent, or if privacy/data-entry burden exceeds benefit.
PROVISIONAL VERDICTS: FOOD-02 NARROW, now subhypothesis FOOD-02C “promotion-framed perishable overbuying” advances to INDIA OFFER-PREVALENCE AUDIT, NOT a validated food-waste intervention. FOOD-01 ADVANCE TO COMPARATIVE TEST, now explicitly stratified by uncertainty in household dinner attendance. Confidence HIGH in randomized Swedish purchase-quantity effect; LOW–MEDIUM in reported nonconsumption effect; HIGH in the mathematical paper as a model, LOW in transfer to Indian real outcomes; VERY LOW in residual GenAI need. Strongest fatal objection: single-unit price transparency, plain nudge and rolling-horizon rules already solve any observed decision at lower cost; alternatively the main barrier is actual product freshness, family behavior or platform incentives. Problem Value /100 WITHHELD: severity of residual segment, Indian frequency, actual waste mass, workaround cost, integration access and AI-specific advantage UNKNOWN. Hackathon 40/25/25/10 NOT SCORED; technical promise conditional on genuine context integration and measured improvement.


14 October 2026: New evidence suggests a possible missing expiry-date information gap. Validation remains pending.


FOOD-02D | Original survey: LocalCircles, 22 June 2026. Of 17,133 Indian online shoppers answering its date-visibility question, 35% said they found best-before dates on no apps, and 13% on only a few. The publisher aggregates these to 48% reporting poor date visibility. Source: https://www.localcircles.com/a/press/page/ecommerce-best-before-date-non-compliance . The survey is self-selected, not nationally representative; it did not weigh discarded food.


Competitor evidence: The same June 2026 report shows selected listings with dates on BigBasket, Amazon Now and Flipkart Minutes, and selected listings without them on Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart, JioMart and Milkbasket. This is NOT a systematic platform-wide audit. An item’s nominal shelf-life duration does not identify the actual batch delivered. NoWaste, Samsung Food, shared lists and ordinary Gemini can only reason reliably about known dates, not undisclosed merchant batch data.


Regulatory uncertainty: FSSAI December 2024 advisory reiterates a remaining-shelf-life delivery standard (30% or 45 days); this is different from display of an exact date before checkout. LocalCircles reports unresolved responsibility for online date disclosure between regulators. Do not make a legal noncompliance determination from survey screenshots. Official advisory: https://fssai.gov.in/upload/advisories/2024/12/674efa161d756Adobe%20Scan%203%20Dec%202024.pdf .


Non-AI baseline: Anzman-Frasca et al., Appetite 218:108397 (online Nov 2025; issue Mar 2026), US pilot RCT with 69 families of children aged 2–5. Editable prefilled healthy carts plus recipes improved the Healthy Eating Index of all household purchases by 5.4%, versus an 8.3% decline in recipes-only controls (p<0.01). Study-store-only difference not significant. This measured purchase nutrition, NOT food waste. Original: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41297859/ . AI not required for editable defaults.


Falsification test NOT RUN: audit 60–100 perishable packaged SKUs in one Indian metro across grocery channels, recording listing dates, actual received batch date (consented purchases), storage, consumption, weighed avoidable edible discard, refund outcome and user effort. Compare accurate simple date disclosure and reminders with NoWaste/Samsung Food/shared lists, ordinary Gemini, and only later a consented agent. No authorized merchant batch feed or checkout integration established.


DECISION: FOOD-02D ADVANCE TO SKU DATA-AVAILABILITY AUDIT ONLY; FOOD-02 overall NARROW; FOOD-01 ADVANCE TO COMPARATIVE VALIDATION (unchanged). Strongest rejection: the core bottleneck is missing merchant batch data or basic disclosure, not GenAI reasoning; or no incremental edible food is wasted. Social/environmental impact and AI advantage remain unmeasured. Problem Value /100 and hackathon 40/25/25/10 scores WITHHELD. Confidence: medium for reported consumer perceptions, low for causal food waste and platform-wide claims.


14 October 2026 — Lane 1 evidence update: An openly published IIT Delhi physical household food-waste dataset is now identified: https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/4gdpmmk2yy/1 (29 Oct 2024, CC BY 4.0). Its archive describes 56 South Delhi households with seven days of sorted waste, 14 food categories, anonymized household data and an interview protocol; 17 high-waste households were interviewed. The archive files have NOT been downloaded or audited; no order receipts or quick-commerce channel linkage is established. Next: inspect exact dataset schema and measure edible waste by category, without inventing a q-commerce effect. FOOD-01 ADVANCE to data audit; FOOD-02 NARROW pending channel-linked waste evidence. Scores withheld.


14 October 2026 — Lane 1 follow-on evidence and falsification notes (new sources).
Bengaluru online/offline fresh-produce channel study: Bharathi et al., 2025, Indian Journal of Agricultural Marketing 39(1), n=160 (80 online, 80 offline), conjoint analysis. Offline buyers ranked purchasing frequency first, then price and place; online buyers ranked platform first, then commodity type. Source: https://econpapers.repec.org/article/agsinjagm/400048.htm ; DOI 10.22004/ag.econ.400048 . This is preference evidence, not measured waste. Implication: quick-commerce-only purchase capture misses market/kirana channels; hypothesis of duplicate buying requires all-channel records. Confidence MEDIUM for the sample, LOW for generalization.
Hyderabad fruit/vegetable e-commerce perceptions: Deepthi et al., 30 Jan 2025, n=100 purposively selected, highlighted product quality concerns. https://eelet.org.uk/index.php/journal/article/view/2495 . No measured spoilage or discarded food. Treat poor freshness on arrival separately from consumer overbuying. Confidence LOW-MEDIUM.
Non-GenAI competitor: Ghuriani et al., published 29 Dec 2025, Indian cross-sectional survey n=341; conventional ML classifiers predicted surveyed waste-related behavior. Authors report 12% improved prediction accuracy after adding food/home management and related variables; abstract does not clarify relative vs absolute percentage. No weighed waste reduction, no tested intervention. https://archive.conscientiabeam.com/index.php/58/article/view/4625 . Confidence MEDIUM for reported prediction result, LOW for impact inference.

Compare (0) cook-visible use-first shelf + practical printed substitution/freezing tips + one WhatsApp cook/diner confirmation + shared Calendar cutoff + deterministic portion rules, (1) ordinary Gemini given identical VERIFIED stock and dietary/safety constraints, (2) NoWaste and Samsung Food only where actual accessible functionality can be tested, and (3) structured Gemini + Google ADK + consented Firestore events. Do not advantage ADK by giving it more reliable inventory or permissions than controls.


POSSIBLE INCREMENTAL GENAI (UNPROVEN): With each participant's explicit opt-in, Gemini structures the cook's Hindi/English message, recipe and confirmed ingredients, asks clarification about missing quantities, dietary restrictions and freezing feasibility, then proposes a NO-PURCHASE substitution and a minimal top-up option with uncertainty. Deterministic code validates units/portion quantities and that no cart line is added without explicit user choice. Firestore records source, who confirmed the change, timestamps, expiry uncertainty, manual corrections and deletion; opt-out flatmates' messages are NOT ingested. Grounded retrieval can cite verified cooking/storage guidance but cannot decide safe edibility. ADK may coordinate a human-confirmed draft, not independently checkout. Swiggy's official 27 JAN 2026 MCP press release https://www.swiggy.com/corporate/press-release/swiggy-now-lets-you-order-food-dineout-and-shop-on-instamart-directly-inside-chatgpt-and-claude/ confirms Swiggy/Instamart servers exist; OUR developer authorization, scopes, effective checkout and user credentials remain UNVERIFIED. No other platform API or live cart assumed; preview/mock only, and human purchase confirmation mandatory.


FALSIFIABLE GATE — NOT RUN: Propose four additional A-lane gold-case variants (NOT edits to common benchmark): missing ingredient but verified acceptable substitute; diner cancellation with cooked food and known safe freezing option; cancellation with unknown storage/freezer capacity (must ask/abstain); recipe suggestion that would trigger an avoidable new perishable purchase. Give all comparators the SAME verified facts. Record whether decision reaches authorized cook in time, safe/acceptable substitutions, unapproved item additions, purchase draft lines, questions, correction/setup minutes, false-confidence/permission failures, p95 latency and cost. A scripted case can only show task correctness. In a later permissioned India field study, record actual shopper/cook/diner actions, receipt vs received quantity across kiranas and all digital channels, cook-start/plan-change time, frozen quantity later consumed vs discarded, purchased edible kg, separately physically weighed avoidable edible grams/household-week and g/kg acquired, INR discarded net of fees/refunds, freezer/storage energy scenario and extra packaging. PASS only if a frequent consequential residual failure survives practical tips + shared messages + incumbents + ordinary Gemini, AND structured workflow reduces mistakes or burden without unsafe claims; physical impact requires a measured comparative study. FAIL/REJECT AI hypothesis if low-tech cooking guidance achieves comparable substitution/freezing/decision quality with lower effort, or extra suggestions increase unconsumed purchases, privacy/food-safety risk or upkeep.


STRONGEST REJECTION: This may be a cooking-skills and household-habit gap already addressed by ordinary instruction, simple substitutions, freezer practices and current recipe tools; there is no evidence that another agent creates net edible-kg savings, and storage or actual consumption may be the limiting factor. DECISION FOOD-01L NARROW to the moment-of-cooking substitution/freeze/buy choice; FOOD-01 overall ADVANCE ONLY TO FAIR COMPARATIVE VALIDATION. FOOD-02O DEFER any inference that quick-commerce frequency, small top-ups or ingredient substitutions cause food waste; FOOD-02 overall NARROW. Problem Value /100 WITHHELD (India frequency/severity/residual/data rights unmeasured). Official 40% GenAI technical, 25% impact, 25% innovation, 10% UX SEPARATELY NOT SCORED: technical feasibility conditional, impact unmeasured, incumbent recipe novelty weak, added burden uncertain. No real accounts, user artifacts, benchmarks, purchases, integrations, waste measurements or impact claimed.

﻿LANE 1 — HOUSEHOLD + QUICK COMMERCE
Start 14 Oct 2026 | India metro-first | Ownership: This document only
Mission: falsify or substantiate FOOD-01 and FOOD-02 at the actual household-decision level. Study purchases, kitchen inventory, delivery, family members' plans, food consumed and actually weighed edible waste. B2C/partner route is secondary to harm. Read Research Control Room before each run.


HYPOTHESIS FOOD-01 — MULTI-PERSON FOOD COORDINATION
People: independent grocery shopper(s), cook, parents, roommates, elders, children, food-delivery consumer; decisions shift after work, school, visitor or meal cancellation. Current evidence: Delhi 56-household audit documents planning, overcooking and changed routines as drivers. Claim of unresolved software gap: UNPROVEN. Compete with NoWaste, Samsung Food, WhatsApp/shared list/calendar and ordinary Gemini. Tests: actual episodes, user effort/time, measurable edible kg; do not assume system can know fridge contents without evidence.


HYPOTHESIS FOOD-02 — QUICK-COMMERCE RELATION TO WASTE
Platforms to inspect: Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, BigBasket/bbnow; plus Swiggy/Zomato restaurant ordering, kiranas and supermarkets. Redseer FY2024 ~6 orders/month among monthly transacting quick-commerce users; metro skew; data does not demonstrate waste consequences. Counter-hypothesis: rapid small orders could reduce overbuying, while promotion-driven extras may increase waste. Need purchase & discard measures with denominator and confounder awareness. Shopping integration/auto checkout is speculative without authentic authorized APIs + consent.


RESEARCH QUEUE
1. Deep incumbent feature audit with dated official documentation and independent complaints if corroborated.
2. Scope authentic anonymized multi-channel household purchase artifacts and feasible consent process.
3. Identify real-life disruption cases with observed duplicate buys, overcooking and wasted perishables; find credible empirical studies (India, Japan, Singapore, Australia, other JAPAC).
4. Evaluate AI orchestration, memory/state (consented), tool calling, voice/image/receipts, grounded healthy/sustainable choices, price comparisons; contrast deterministic rules and ordinary LLM.
5. Falsification: if baseline shared-list/NoWaste/Samsung Food performs equivalently in real cases, downgrade. Measure edible kg, cost, effort and retention, not engagement only.


CURRENT VERDICT: FOOD-01 ADVANCE TO COMPARATIVE TEST; FOOD-02 NARROW CAUSAL EVIDENCE UNKNOWN. Benchmark NOT RUN.
SOURCE STARTERS
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0950329325003064
https://redseer.com/articles/indias-q-commerce-ascent-a-new-era-in-shopping/
https://www.nowasteapp.com/home/
https://support.samsungfood.com/hc/en-us/articles/35369657798548-Getting-Started-with-Meal-Planner
https://www.swiggy.com/corporate/press-release/how-india-swiggyd-2025-a-feast-for-the-fast-the-foodie-and-the-future/
APPEND DATED RUN ENTRIES BELOW. Keep earlier findings and counterfindings; no fabricated tests.




14 OCT 2026 — LANE 1, RUN 01: NEW EVIDENCE AND RESEARCH DECISIONS
FOOD-02: QUICK COMMERCE MUST BE SEGMENTED BY PURCHASE MISSION. A Grant Thornton Bharat 2026 survey, reported by PTI on 7 April, covered over 1,600 consumers and 1,000 kirana retailers in Indian metros and smaller cities. Reported usage motives: 45% urgent purchases, 24% daily top-ups, 19% impulse purchases. These are survey responses, not measured waste, and original questionnaire/weighting was not available. Source: https://money.rediff.com/amp/news/market/convenience-drives-retail-choices-in-india-report/44897720260407 . Hypothesis: urgent top-ups may reduce bulk spoilage; impulse buying may have different effects. No causal evidence yet. Verdict: NARROW. Kill if real discarded edible food does not differ after controlling for household characteristics.


FOOD-02 FRESH PRODUCE CHANNELS: LocalCircles original survey published 24 Nov 2023, fielded Sep–Nov 2023, >24,000 question responses across 297 Indian districts. Of 12,207 respondents asked where they bought MOST household fruits and vegetables, only 7% chose online grocery, while 45% chose local markets, 21% weekly markets and 19% neighbourhood vendors. Among 11,964 responses to a separate multiple-choice online-produce problems question, 73% selected low quality, 56% high prices, 51% difficult returns, 37% inconsistent availability. Source: https://www.localcircles.com/a/press/page/grocery-platforms-survey . Caveat: self-selected platform respondents; 2023, not a 2026 population estimate. The 7% is PRIMARY channel, not whether respondents ever buy online. Complaints are not measured spoilage. This challenges an app centered only on online order receipts. Potential unmet failure: short-lived produce arriving in poor condition, but supplier quality/returns rather than GenAI may dominate. Verdict: NARROW. Proposed falsification (NOT RUN): 30 paired produce purchase lines from delivery and local markets, recording arrival condition, shelf life, consumed/discarded edible grams, price, and existing refund outcome. Kill if actual discard is unaffected or ordinary quality control is adequate.


FOOD-02 ADJACENT ENVIRONMENTAL LEVER: Eshtiyagh et al. (preprint 21 Oct 2025) analyzed 6,362,860 express grocery orders from Dubai (2023) and 2,169,520 scheduled orders (2022), total 8,532,380. A dispatch/bundling simulation using these records estimated that about five additional minutes could reduce daily delivery mileage by ~30% and modeled lifecycle carbon emissions by ~20% in tested conditions. This was not an observed intervention, an India estimate, a reduction in discarded food, or a demonstrated AI benefit. Peer review unconfirmed. Original: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19066 . Verdict: NARROW as a logistics-emissions hypothesis separate from food waste. Main objection: established operations-research routing may be sufficient; household apps lack dispatch authority.


Research status: FOOD-02 remains NARROW; food waste effect unmeasured.


Further counterevidence: Existing grocery services already provide scheduled delivery choices in some locations. Delivery-window selection is not itself a novel product feature. The original source was a September 2026 industry report; availability in the selected metro needs verification. Conventional routing remains the baseline comparator.


Next research gate (NOT RUN): collect consented grocery purchase receipts, purchase mission, changes in household meal plans and weighed edible discard for a small urban household sample. Compare results against ordinary shared lists, NoWaste, Samsung Food and a general LLM. Analyze actual food discarded rather than order counts. Track grocery spending, time burden and any delivery-emissions scenario separately. FOOD-01 remains ADVANCE TO COMPARATIVE TEST; FOOD-02 remains NARROW. Strongest kill criterion: no meaningful residual failure beyond existing tools, or purchase channel does not predict avoidable waste after accounting for household differences. Project Problem Value /100 and judging scores withheld until this is tested.




14 OCT 2026 — LANE 1, RUN 02: ONLINE VEGETABLE SHOPPING AND THE FIRST-WASTE EVENT (NEW ORIGINAL EVIDENCE)


PRIMARY NEW FINDING — FOOD-02: A PEER-REVIEWED CHANNEL COMPARISON FINDS AN ASSOCIATION WITH MORE VEGETABLE WASTE, BUT NOT A QUICK-COMMERCE CAUSAL EFFECT.
Tian, Lin, Gao, Yu and Li, “From markets to clicks: The impact of purchasing channel migration on household food waste,” Waste Management 204:114908; published online 29 May 2025, issue 1 Aug 2025, DOI 10.1016/j.wasman.2025.114908. Original source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40446430/ . Geography: China, household vegetable consumption. Abstract reports online purchases associated with +12.967 grams vegetable waste, +0.017 waste proportion, and +0.121 higher probability of ANY waste compared with offline purchasing. The association was statistically apparent for leafy and root vegetables, not fruit vegetables. Increased risk of waste attributed to expiration (+0.125) and improper storage (+0.072) in the model. Crucially, among households that ALREADY wasted vegetables, there was no significant difference in waste amount/proportion between purchasing channels. This suggests the actionable hypothesis might be preventing the first avoidable spoilage incident, rather than reducing waste volume among all existing wasters.


EVIDENCE LIMITS: Full article methodology and sampling denominator not accessible in this research pass: UNKNOWN; units/time base of +12.967 g not sufficiently specified in the abstract; DO NOT present it as grams per household-week/order or extrapolate it to India. The abstract uses causal language, but identification strategy and selection/confounding controls cannot be independently audited here. Online grocery in China is NOT identical to 10-minute quick commerce in India. 0.121 is a model-reported probability change, not a measured India quick-commerce effect. No physical weighing method was verified from abstract; classify measurement mode UNKNOWN. Evidence confidence MEDIUM for reported study findings, LOW for India causal transfer.


NEW RESEARCH QUESTION / SPECIFIC USER TASK: A metro grocery buyer receives online leafy/root vegetables; other household members decide meals, and produce remains unused because shelf-life and storage decisions were not aligned with changing meal attendance. Can a household reliably identify and act on a vulnerable batch BEFORE the first spoilage event, beyond a receipt reminder, simple storage label, shared list, NoWaste or Samsung Food? Current evidence supports possible failure at storage/expiration, NOT that cross-app ordering is its cause. A photo alone cannot certify freshness or remaining safe shelf life.


INDEPENDENT BEHAVIORAL CORROBORATION, DISTINCT CHANNEL: Shamim and Misra, “Unravelling the dynamics of food waste and food delivery apps: insights from SEM and FSQCA,” British Food Journal 127(11):4077–4091 (2025), DOI 10.1108/BFJ-11-2024-1226, publisher issue: https://www.emerald.com/bfj/issue/127/11 ; indexed abstract: https://ouci.dntb.gov.ua/en/works/7WjmqN1L/ . Sample: 344 online food-delivery app users, online survey; geography NOT verified in accessible abstract. Structural equation modeling finds hedonic value associated with over-ordering, which is associated with reported food waste; personalization associated with hedonic value but not functional value. This concerns PREPARED MEAL DELIVERY, not online groceries or household inventory; self-report/SEM associations are NOT verified grams or proof that platform design causes waste. It independently suggests an additional purchase-stage behavioral mechanism but must not be combined with the vegetable-waste coefficient. Evidence confidence MEDIUM for described correlations, LOW for causal interpretation or transfer to Indian metros.


COMPETITION AND COUNTEREVIDENCE: NoWaste and Samsung Food already advertise expiry reminders, inventory, shopping lists, meal planning and recipe recommendations; WhatsApp and shared calendars handle changing attendance, and ordinary Gemini can explain storage guidelines and suggest ingredient use. Traditional refrigerator organization in the 2025 Japan 119-household intervention performed at least comparably to an app in short-run waste reduction; do not assume AI outperforms physical visibility. Online top-up purchasing might reduce bulk spoilage, and Chinese channel associations could reflect buyer selection, product quality or packaging. Existing apps may already address the proposed incident; no head-to-head run.


AI ROLE (CONDITIONAL, NOT A SOLUTION COMMITMENT): Gemini could reconcile user-consented purchase artifacts, household schedule changes and structured product facts, maintain auditable per-item state, invoke permitted reminder/checkout tools with explicit authorization, and ground food-storage advice in authoritative sources. Actual spoilage-risk thresholds, purchased quantities, dates and budget should use verified data plus deterministic rules. A standard reminder or visible refrigerator organizer is the baseline; agents/memory only matter if they demonstrably reduce missed interventions and user effort. No official general consumer checkout integration with Blinkit/Zepto/Instamart verified; automation remains blocked on access/authorization. No new Gemini feature tested.


FALSIFIABLE STUDY DESIGN — NOT RUN: 15–30 consenting Indian metro households over 3–4 weeks, ideally pre-registered, capturing online/offline vegetable batches separately (leafy, root, fruit vegetables), purchase weight/price/channel/date, freshness at arrival, packaging/storage, planned vs actual meals, edible grams discarded with reason/date and actual consumption. Compare (A) ordinary shared list + visible storage guidance, (B) NoWaste/Samsung Food or equivalent, (C) ordinary Gemini conversation, and (D) any new workflow ONLY after it is built; use within-household comparisons or randomization if feasible, not mere cross-sectional channel correlation. Primary outcome: probability of any avoidable edible spoilage event per purchased produce batch and grams wasted / grams purchased; secondary: grams/household-week, INR discarded, household time/steps, accuracy of item state, and any net environmental savings estimated conservatively by produce category and disposal path. Control for household size, storage, purchased quantity, product quality and cooking frequency. This is a PROPOSED test, not evidence that data or participants exist.


DECISION: FOOD-02 stays NARROW but now has a specific independent published signal for online vegetable expiration/storage; FOOD-01 stays ADVANCE TO COMPARATIVE TEST because multi-person coordination remains plausible but unproven after incumbent tools. Do NOT advance to an automated purchasing product or score /100: frequency of residual unmet incident, workaround cost, data access, actual effect and GenAI advantage remain UNKNOWN. Hackathon 40/25/25/10 readiness also NOT SCORED. Strongest rejection: basic storage guidance, fridge organization or existing apps perform equally well, or product quality/household behavior dominates information, so an AI workflow cannot credibly prevent discarded edible grams. Revisit only with genuine Indian paired purchase-to-disposal evidence or a valid incumbent comparison.


14 OCT 2026 — LANE 1 RUN 03: NEW EVIDENCE — INDIA ONLINE GROCERY OVER-ORDERING
Jasrotia et al., SN Business & Economics 6(10), October 2026, DOI 10.1007/s43546-026-01458-1; https://ideas.repec.org/a/spr/snbeco/v6y2026i10d10.1007_s43546-026-01458-1.html . Original Indian survey of 363 online grocery shoppers analyzed by PLS-SEM found perceived value associated with impulse buying and over-ordering; wider assortment and price value related to perceived value. Convenience moderation was not supported. This is an India-specific purchase mechanism, NOT measured edible food waste, not quick-commerce-specific, not a representative household sample, and not causal experimental evidence. Full methods inaccessible here. Confidence MEDIUM for survey associations, LOW for discarded-food inference. FOOD-02 NARROW: test whether promotion-driven over-orders of perishable food are actually discarded, after comparing urgent/top-up orders, kirana and supermarket purchases. Strongest rejection: purchases are consumed or stockpiled and do not create additional avoidable food waste.


14 OCT 2026 — LANE 1 RUN 03: NEW NON-GENAI CONTROL AND EVIDENCE GATE
Seta et al., “Effects of a gamified self-monitoring app on household food waste reduction,” Detritus 35:23–41, available online 26 May 2026; original journal https://digital.detritusjournal.com/articles/effects-of-a-gamified-self-monitoring-app-on-household-food-waste-reduction/5732 ; DOI 10.31025/2611-4135/2026.19596 . Japan intervention involving 126 households assigned to intervention/control, with cloud-connected weighing of separately discarded avoidable food across three two-week measurement periods (baseline, intervention, three-month follow-up). A non-GenAI gamified behavior app prompted searching for food needing use, moving it visibly, using it and finishing meals. Reported average weekly household avoidable waste fell by 190 g (45%) in intervention vs 60 g (13%) control, a 32-percentage-point difference in within-group percentage declines, not a demonstrated AI saving. Baseline-adjusted bootstrap GLM found a statistically significant intervention/control difference. Abstract does NOT resolve long-term follow-up persistence or which behavior mediated the result; behavior-change indicators were not significantly associated with waste changes in the main-effects model. Over 90% of intervention participants used the app five or more days per week, but long-run adoption is unknown. Confidence HIGH for sample's physically measured contrast, LOW for generalizing to Indian metros or proving GenAI value. This is a stronger competitor than a generic inventory app and raises the evidence bar for FOOD-01.
Independent adjacent mechanism, NOT pooled with groceries: Rahman et al., Food and Humanity 5:100886 (Dec 2025), DOI 10.1016/j.foohum.2025.100886, original university publication https://scholar.ub.ac.id/en/publications/do-online-food-delivery-platforms-contribute-to-food-waste-eviden/ . Cross-sectional model using 1,042 Indonesian university respondents associated prepared-meal delivery frequency with reported waste and over-ordering; this is not Indian quick commerce, not verified physical weights, and not randomized causal evidence.
Next falsification (NOT RUN): For consenting metro households compare real purchase motives (urgent/top-up vs promotion/impulse) and low-tech use-first refrigerator zones/basic reminders vs NoWaste/Samsung Food/shared lists and ordinary Gemini, recording receipt quantity, purchase price, meal changes, actual edible grams discarded per purchased edible gram, first spoilage events per batch, time spent and fridge conditions. Only test a proposed Gemini agent after baseline alternatives; use grounded structured data, consented household state and explicit authorization for any external checkout. Rules may outperform an agent for expiry reminders and duplicate purchases. No partner checkout API, study participants or product effects verified. FOOD-01 ADVANCE TO COMPARATIVE VALIDATION; FOOD-02 NARROW, causality unresolved. Problem Value /100 and official 40/25/25/10 hackathon scores WITHHELD. Strongest FOOD-01 rejection: simple visibility and habit changes match any AI approach at lower effort; strongest FOOD-02 rejection: no incremental edible discard after adjusting for household traits and item quality.




14 OCT 2026 — LANE 1 RUN 04: CAUSAL PROMOTION EXPERIMENT + SHOPPING-FREQUENCY COUNTERMODEL (NEW EVIDENCE)
FOOD-02 NEW STRONGER ORIGINAL EVIDENCE: MULTI-UNIT PROMOTIONS CAN CAUSE EXTRA PERISHABLE PURCHASES, BUT DIRECT PHYSICAL FOOD-WASTE IMPACT REMAINS UNMEASURED.
Gravert, Christina and Mormann, Milica, “In-store food promotions increase sales as well as household food waste,” Scientific Reports 15, 18035, published 23 May 2025. ORIGINAL OPEN ARTICLE: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-01800-x . Underlying public data and analysis code: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/7NSBP (authors report availability; files NOT downloaded or audited here). Actual natural field experiment: eight supermarkets from two chains in SWEDEN, 8–21 March 2021, with 43,246 units of cucumber/broccoli sold. The article was published in 2025; data were collected in 2021. Retail displays were randomized across store/time in an A-B-A design, with the same effective unit price. Multi-unit “2 for X” framing increased units sold by 19.5% relative to “1 for X/2” (p<0.001). A simple consumption-oriented prompt reduced units purchased 10.8% vs multi-unit framing, and a salient single-item comparison price reduced units 9.1% (both p<0.001). These are SALES quantity changes, NOT measured avoided food waste. Critically, simple non-AI nudges worked, setting a high bar for any GenAI cart advisor.
Follow-up: QR stickers were attached to 21,000 vegetables; 178 shoppers completed a one-week consumption follow-up (~1% response); 176 retained after excluding two who said they bought zero. Of the 121 respondents buying at least two items, 12% in the multi-unit condition vs 0% in the single-unit-discount condition reported not fully consuming purchased food (p=0.064, so NOT significant at conventional 5% threshold); 15% prompt and 6% salience groups also reported not fully consuming. This was self-reported BINARY full consumption, not weighed edible waste, and does NOT definitively establish food disposal; low follow-up response and small treatment cells limit waste inference. A separate preregistered US online hypothetical shopping experiment recruited 397, analyzed 389 after attention check; respondents given two-for-one broccoli scenario rated perceived waste likelihood 54.73/100 vs 42.07/100 for a single broccoli at 50% discount (p=0.021), and 34.19/100 for one regular-priced (p<0.001). This is INTENTION/PERCEIVED RISK, not physical waste. Strong causal evidence for PURCHASE framing effect, weaker for actual disposal, and no direct Indian q-commerce evidence.
RESEARCH INTERPRETATION (NOT A RESULT): The key decision may be “Should I add a second short-shelf-life unit because of an offer?” rather than “What should I cook?” This occurs before purchasing and can be shared across kiranas, supermarkets, Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart, but evidence does not show any named Indian platform deploys the same perishable multi-unit mechanism at scale. Compare offers actually observed in one metro, never infer from platform category or discount campaigns. The retailer has a potential incentive conflict: more units sold vs fewer discarded by households. The cheapest competitor is an accurate per-unit price and one-line “will this be used?” nudge, not a GenAI agent. A platform partner's willingness to change cart design is UNKNOWN.
FOOD-01 + FOOD-02 IMPORTANT CONTRARIAN 2025 MODEL: van Rooijen, Gerdessen, Claassen and de Leeuw, “Meal planning under uncertainty: How shopping frequency affects food waste,” Sustainable Production and Consumption 57:403–412, published July 2025; original university record https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/meal-planning-under-uncertainty-how-shopping-frequency-affects-fo/ ; DOI https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spc.2025.05.015 ; full open repository PDF https://edepot.wur.nl/694932 . The researchers built a ROLLING-HORIZON MATHEMATICAL OPTIMIZATION model of a four-person household over 21 days with low, medium and high uncertainty in dinner attendance, considering package sizes, nutrition and recipe selection. Across shopping frequencies, MODELLED food waste ranged 0–52 g, 46–300 g and 50–900 g per 21 days for low/medium/high uncertainty, respectively; these are scenario outputs, NOT measured household waste or real-world effect sizes. In the model, more frequent shopping can reduce waste when meal attendance is uncertain, while less frequent coordinated shopping may suit stable households. Selecting recipes based on existing stock reduced simulated waste to about 3 g/day across uncertainty levels. Thus “frequent q-commerce is wasteful” is an invalid blanket assumption. A conditional choice of shopping frequency and quantities is a more defensible research question. The paper demonstrates NON-GENAI operations research already covers a large part of the decision logic, so any Gemini advantage must be in collecting changing attendance/intent with less friction and connecting reliable context, not mathematical meal optimization alone.
NEW CROSS-SOURCE INSIGHT: The 2025 Swedish randomized purchase-framing experiment supports a causal retail decision lever, while the 2025 Netherlands mathematical model supports a countervailing benefit from flexible small purchases under uncertain meal attendance. These are different countries, settings, methods and outcome types; they cannot be pooled into a single expected India reduction or carbon figure. Combined, they argue for a nuanced taxonomy: (A) demand-matched urgent top-up; (B) deliberate multi-day stock-up; (C) promotion-induced extra perishables; (D) planned short-life markdown purchase. Only category C has the new controlled promotion evidence, and even there physically weighed waste remains UNKNOWN.
COMPETITION: NoWaste and Samsung Food already provide pantry lists, meal planning and inventory features; WhatsApp/Calendar communicate attendance, ordinary Gemini can reason about quantity and offer arithmetic. The Swedish trial shows a plain unit-price display and text nudge can alter purchasing; Wageningen shows deterministic rolling-horizon optimization can model uncertain meal demand. A differentiator requiring GenAI/agents/memory is NOT established. An authorized purchase or cart-modification API for Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart, BigBasket or Swiggy/Zomato has NOT been verified; no automatic buying should be claimed.
MEASUREMENT AND ACCESS: The Gravert/Mormann authors explicitly publish underlying experiment data/code on OSF (access/rights to be checked before use); this enables reproducibility of purchase effects, NOT Indian grocery waste. No Indian household consented receipts, offer screenshots, purchase/consumption logs or weighed edible disposal records available yet. To evaluate environmental/social severity measure edible grams discarded / edible grams purchased by category, INR paid for discarded food, meal attendance uncertainty, effort, package size, and actual delivery/packaging footprint. For any CO2e/water use food- and region-specific factors and counterfactual substitution; do not count reduced purchases as automatically reduced emissions without inventory response.
FALSIFIABLE NEXT TEST (NOT RUN): (1) Audit 100 current real perishable offer cards from one selected Indian metro across quick commerce AND kiranas/supermarkets, recording actual single vs multi-unit effective unit price, quantity constraints, expiration/freshness, promo type and whether cart controls can be changed; platform terms respected, no scraping. (2) Recruit consenting households with varying meal-attendance uncertainty; track purchase intent, order receipts, actual edible grams consumed/discarded per item/batch over 3–4 weeks. (3) Compare randomized basic unit-price + one-line nudge against existing inventory app/shared list and ordinary Gemini; only then test a consented context-aware agent. (4) Pre-register two distinct hypotheses: promotions increase quantity (purchase effect) and promotions increase physically discarded edible mass (waste effect), accounting for actual package size, price, freshness and meal attendance. Reject if India offers lack multi-unit framing, if added food is consumed, if simple nudge is equivalent, or if privacy/data-entry burden exceeds benefit.
PROVISIONAL VERDICTS: FOOD-02 NARROW, now subhypothesis FOOD-02C “promotion-framed perishable overbuying” advances to INDIA OFFER-PREVALENCE AUDIT, NOT a validated food-waste intervention. FOOD-01 ADVANCE TO COMPARATIVE TEST, now explicitly stratified by uncertainty in household dinner attendance. Confidence HIGH in randomized Swedish purchase-quantity effect; LOW–MEDIUM in reported nonconsumption effect; HIGH in the mathematical paper as a model, LOW in transfer to Indian real outcomes; VERY LOW in residual GenAI need. Strongest fatal objection: single-unit price transparency, plain nudge and rolling-horizon rules already solve any observed decision at lower cost; alternatively the main barrier is actual product freshness, family behavior or platform incentives. Problem Value /100 WITHHELD: severity of residual segment, Indian frequency, actual waste mass, workaround cost, integration access and AI-specific advantage UNKNOWN. Hackathon 40/25/25/10 NOT SCORED; technical promise conditional on genuine context integration and measured improvement.


14 October 2026: New evidence suggests a possible missing expiry-date information gap. Validation remains pending.


FOOD-02D | Original survey: LocalCircles, 22 June 2026. Of 17,133 Indian online shoppers answering its date-visibility question, 35% said they found best-before dates on no apps, and 13% on only a few. The publisher aggregates these to 48% reporting poor date visibility. Source: https://www.localcircles.com/a/press/page/ecommerce-best-before-date-non-compliance . The survey is self-selected, not nationally representative; it did not weigh discarded food.


Competitor evidence: The same June 2026 report shows selected listings with dates on BigBasket, Amazon Now and Flipkart Minutes, and selected listings without them on Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart, JioMart and Milkbasket. This is NOT a systematic platform-wide audit. An item’s nominal shelf-life duration does not identify the actual batch delivered. NoWaste, Samsung Food, shared lists and ordinary Gemini can only reason reliably about known dates, not undisclosed merchant batch data.

Questionnaires before and 1 and 6 months after intervention. Reported significant increases in behaviors in the intervention group included substituting missing recipe ingredients with available foods, freezing dishes not immediately eaten, and using normally discarded edible vegetable parts; frequency of reported food disposal also declined. Control participants also improved, and the additional waste-awareness material produced comparable effects to practical tips alone. ABSTRACT DOES NOT REPORT edible grams weighed, p values, episode denominators, between-arm numerical effect sizes, randomization, or India-specific outcomes. Confidence HIGH for publication/sample sizes/design as reported; MEDIUM for self-reported direction; LOW for extrapolation to Indian multi-person paid-cook/flatmate homes.

WHY MATERIAL / CAUSALITY: The failure is the POST-CHANGE action, not just meal RSVP or pantry capture: use existing food via a permitted substitution; freeze appropriate excess with user-verified handling; OR buy only a confirmed missing item. Cooking-class evidence supports practical non-AI behavior change as a serious baseline and suggests education at the cooking moment can help. It does NOT show that AI, freezing or any quick-commerce channel reduces food waste. Freezing is not avoided waste unless food is subsequently consumed, and an extra small top-up may be efficient if it completes a meal. A change after cooking may still be salvageable for future meals, but food safety, storage conditions, freezer capacity and household preferences must be confirmed by humans; no photo/model may certify safe edibility. Environmental gains need measured net food displacement, storage energy, packaging/delivery and credible factors.
